I regolatori della CPU gestiscono il modo in cui il dispositivo regola la frequenza della CPU per bilanciare prestazioni e consumo energetico. Ecco una rapida panoramica:

• Walt: un regolatore sviluppato da Google ottimizzato per la reattività e la latenza dell'interazione dell'utente, utilizzato principalmente nei dispositivi Pixel.
• Conservativo: aumenta gradualmente la frequenza della CPU; consente di risparmiare batteria ma può ridurre la reattività.
• risparmio energetico: mantiene la CPU alla frequenza più bassa possibile, dando priorità alla durata della batteria rispetto alle prestazioni.
• prestazioni: blocca la CPU alla massima frequenza, garantendo le massime prestazioni a scapito della batteria.
• schedhorizon: un governatore sensibile allo scheduler che mira a migliorare la migrazione delle attività e l'efficienza tra i core.
• schedutil: il governatore moderno predefinito in molti kernel; utilizza i dati dello scheduler di Linux per scalare la frequenza della CPU in modo intelligente ed efficiente.

zRAM Compression Algorithms Comparison


zRAM (compressed RAM) is a Linux kernel feature that allows RAM compression to store more data in memory, thereby reducing swap (paging) usage to disk. The most common compression algorithms are LZ4, LZO, LZO-RLE, and ZSTD. These are compared primarily based on compression ratio, speed (compression/decompression speed), latency, throughput, and CPU usage.

The comparison is based on benchmarks and tests from various sources (e.g., LinuxReviews, Reddit/Fedora, Emin's Notes), typically measured on 1-1.1 GB datasets (e.g., Linux kernel source code). The tests show that algorithm performance depends on hardware (e.g., CPU), workload, and settings (e.g., vm.page-cluster).

Comparative Table (Based on Average Values)

Algorithm Compression Ratio Compression Time (1.1 GB) Decompression Speed (GiB/s) Throughput (MiB/s) Latency (ns) CPU Usage
LZ4 2.58–2.63 ~4.47 s ~12.4 7943–11434 1708–10674 Low
LZO ~2.77 ~4.57 s ~9.31 5821–7496 2428–16426 Medium
LZO-RLE ~2.74 ~4.47 s ~9.78 6264–8248 2235–14897 Medium
ZSTD 3.37–3.97 ~7.90 s ~3.91 2612–3005 5714–41343 High

- Compression Ratio: How much smaller the compressed data is compared to the original (higher is better, e.g., ZSTD can achieve up to 3-4x smaller size).
- Compression Time: Time to compress the data (lower is better).
- Decompression Speed: Speed of decompressing the data (higher is better).
- Throughput: Data processing capacity (higher is better, based on page-cluster=0–3 values).
- Latency: Waiting time in nanoseconds (lower is better).
- CPU Usage: Relative processor load (lower is better for performance).

Analysis: Pros and Cons
- LZ4:
 - Pros: Fastest compression and decompression, low latency and CPU usage. Ideal for frequent swap cases (e.g., games, multitasking), where speed is critical. High throughput and IOPS (up to 2 million operations/s).
 - Cons: Lower compression ratio, so it may use more memory, increasing OOM (out-of-memory) risk under heavy memory pressure.
 - Recommended Setting: vm.page-cluster=1 for balance between latency and throughput.

- LZO:
 - Pros: Good balance between speed and compression, lower CPU demand than ZSTD.
 - Cons: Slower than LZ4 or LZO-RLE, with marginal benefits. Less efficient on modern systems.
 - Recommended Setting: For general use, but often replaced by better alternatives.

- LZO-RLE (LZO Run-Length Encoding):
 - Pros: Faster decompression than LZO, better compression ratio for certain data (e.g., repeating patterns). Similar speed to LZ4.
 - Cons: Slightly weaker throughput than LZ4, and more prone to OOM at high swap activity.
 - Recommended Setting: Default in many kernels (e.g., Fedora), but switching to ZSTD is recommended.

- ZSTD (Zstandard):
 - Pros: Best compression ratio, requiring less swap, reducing memory pressure. Effective for textual data (e.g., logs, browser tabs). In real tests, it completes tasks faster under heavy memory pressure because less data needs to be moved.
 - Cons: Slower compression/decompression, higher latency and CPU usage. Not ideal for frequently accessed data.
 - Recommended Setting: vm.page-cluster=0 to reduce latency (default on ChromeOS/Android). vm.swappiness=180 for more aggressive swap usage.

General Recommendations
- General Use (e.g., desktop, browsing): ZSTD with page-cluster=0 – better compression, less swap, ideal if swapped data is rarely used (e.g., old tabs).
- Performance-Intensive Tasks (e.g., games, servers): LZ4 – faster, lower latency, but may use more memory.
- Old or Weak Hardware: LZO-RLE or LZ4 – lower CPU demand.
- Testing: Try it on your own system (e.g., with zramctl commands), as performance depends on hardware. For example, on Raspberry Pi or ARM devices, ZSTD is more efficient for logs.
- Other: From kernel 5.1, LZO-RLE is the default, but many distributions (e.g., Fedora) switch to ZSTD. Other algorithms (e.g., DEFLATE, 842) exist but are slower and less commonly used in zRAM.

I/O Scheduler Comparison

 I/O (Input/Output) schedulers determine how the system handles read and write requests to storage devices. Different schedulers optimize for different use cases.


Available Schedulers:


- CFQ (Completely Fair Queuing)
 Default on many systems. Provides fair access to all processes. Good balance between throughput and latency.
 Best for: General use, multi-tasking
 Pros: Fair, predictable, good for multiple apps
 Cons: Not optimal for specific workloads


- Deadline
 Guarantees requests are served within a deadline. Prevents request starvation.
 Best for: Databases, real-time apps
 Pros: Low latency, prevents starvation
 Cons: Lower throughput than noop


- NOOP (No Operation)
 Simple FIFO (First In First Out) scheduler. Minimal overhead.
 Best for: SSDs, fast flash storage
 Pros: Very low CPU overhead, good for SSDs
 Cons: No optimization, can cause latency spikes


- BFQ (Budget Fair Queuing)
 Modern scheduler focused on responsiveness and fairness.
 Best for: Interactive workloads, UI responsiveness
 Pros: Excellent responsiveness, low latency
 Cons: Slightly higher CPU usage


- Kyber
 Modern multi-queue scheduler for fast storage.
 Best for: NVMe SSDs, modern hardware
 Pros: Excellent for fast storage, low latency
 Cons: Requires modern kernel support


Recommendations:
 - HDDs: CFQ or Deadline
 - SSDs/Flash: NOOP, BFQ, or Kyber
 - Gaming: BFQ or Deadline
 - General use: CFQ or BFQ
 - Benchmarking: NOOP
